sentence: Pain that comes and goes or does not go away is a reason for a routine GP appointment.
The NHS says pelvic pain is more common in women.
Common causes include period pain, an ovarian cyst, endometriosis and pain related to pregnancy.
Rarer but more serious causes include ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease, womb cancer and ovarian cancer.
Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is an infection of the female reproductive organs.
note: NHS PID page; definition is a textbook gloss

sentence: Most cases start with a sexually transmitted infection such as chlamydia or gonorrhoea.
Bacteria that normally live in the vagina cause some cases.
The NHS suggests booking a GP appointment if pelvic pain comes and goes or does not go away.
Bloating that does not go away, weight loss or changes in bowel habit are further reasons.
Pain during sex, pain when peeing or pooing, and bleeding between periods are also listed.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for pelvic pain with difficulty peeing or pooing, blood in urine or stool, unusual vaginal discharge or bleeding, or a very high temperature.
The same advice applies if the person is or may be pregnant.
For an ovarian cyst, sudden severe pelvic pain is a reason for an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.

sentence: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if pelvic pain is severe, getting worse, or hurts when you move or touch the area.
Fainting or feeling dizzy, pain at the tip of the shoulder, difficulty breathing, heavy vaginal bleeding and sudden confusion are also on the 999 list.
For PID, the NHS says to call 999 or go straight to A&E for severe pelvic pain or heavy vaginal bleeding, and not to drive yourself.
Assessment usually starts with questions and an examination.

sentence: Urine or swab samples, a pregnancy test, and an ultrasound scan, which may be transvaginal, can follow, and an MRI scan of the pelvis is sometimes used.

sentence: There is no single test for PID, and it is diagnosed from symptoms and an examination.
